title: Why Wine in Europe Doesn't Give You a Headache (the Real Reasons)
excerpt: Why does wine in Italy or France not give you a headache? The sulfite myth, US vs EU wine rules, and the real reasons people feel better drinking wine in Europe.
metaDescription: Why wine in Italy or France doesn't give you a headache: the sulfite myth, US vs EU wine rules, and the real reasons, plus how to drink that way at home.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no study showing that European wine causes fewer headaches than American wine, and the most popular explanation, that European wine has no sulfites, is simply wrong. European wine contains sulfites too, and the EU's legal limits on them are only somewhat lower than the US limit. What *is* real is that people drink differently on a trip to Italy or France: slower, with food, in smaller pours, with more water and walking, less stress, and often a little less in total. Those habits, plus a few genuine differences in the wine itself and in labeling rules, explain most of the "I can drink wine in Europe and feel fine" experience.

**The quick takeaways:** If wine gives you headaches at home, the fix is probably not a plane ticket. Drink at a European pace (with a meal, one glass per hour or slower, water between glasses), pay attention to the alcohol percentage on the label, try lighter and less sun-baked styles, and keep a simple log of which wines bother you. If your headaches come on fast after one glass, they're severe, or they come with flushing, hives, or a stuffy nose, the cause may be your own body's response to something in wine, and that's worth raising with a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most wine headaches are an unpleasant but harmless mix of alcohol, dehydration, and poor sleep. **See a doctor if** you get a headache from very small amounts of wine every time, your headaches look like migraines (throbbing on one side, nausea, sensitivity to light), you get hives, wheezing, flushing, or a racing heart after drinking, or you have asthma and notice breathing trouble with wine. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) for** a sudden "worst headache of my life," a headache with confusion, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, a stiff neck, or fever, or swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat. Those are not hangover symptoms.

## Why People Say Wine in Europe Doesn't Give Them a Headache

You've probably heard some version of this story. Someone gets a pounding headache from a glass or two of red at home, then spends two weeks in Tuscany drinking wine with lunch and dinner and wakes up fine every morning. They come home convinced American wine is full of chemicals and European wine is "pure."

The experience is real. People aren't making it up. The question is what's actually causing it, and the answer matters, because if you blame the wrong thing (sulfites, usually) you'll spend money on fixes that don't help.

There are three broad groups of explanations:

1. **Differences in how you drink** when you're traveling, especially in Southern Europe.
2. **Differences in the wine you happen to be drinking**, which are mostly about style, alcohol level, and grape growing conditions, not continent.
3. **Differences in the rules** for what goes in wine and what goes on the label, which are real but smaller than the internet suggests.

Let's take them one at a time, starting with the myth that gets the most attention.

## Does European Wine Have Fewer Sulfites? The Myth vs the Rules

Sulfites (sulfur dioxide and related compounds) are used in winemaking almost everywhere to stop spoilage and oxidation. Yeast also makes a small amount naturally during fermentation, so even wine with no added sulfites isn't completely sulfite-free.

Here's how the rules actually compare:

| | United States | European Union |
|---|---|---|
| Sulfites allowed? | Yes | Yes |
| "Contains sulfites" warning | Required above 10 parts per million (since the late 1980s) | Required above 10 mg per liter (since 2005) |
| Legal maximum (typical dry wine) | 350 parts per million for all wine | About 150 mg/L for dry red, about 200 mg/L for dry white and rosé |
| Maximum for organic wine | "Organic" (USDA) wine allows no added sulfites; "made with organic grapes" allows up to 100 ppm | Lower limits than conventional EU wine, roughly 100 mg/L red, 150 mg/L white |

(Parts per million and milligrams per liter are essentially the same unit for wine, so you can compare the numbers directly.)

So yes, the US ceiling is higher on paper. But a ceiling is not what's in the bottle. Most quality dry wine on both sides of the Atlantic sits well below either limit, because winemakers don't want the burnt-match smell that too much sulfur gives. A typical dry red from California and a typical dry red from Tuscany are likely to be in the same general range.

The other half of the myth is the label. Wine sold in the EU *does* say "contains sulphites" (often in several languages, or with a small icon). Many travelers just don't notice it on a carafe of house wine that has no label at all.

### Why sulfites probably aren't causing your headache anyway

Even if European wine had dramatically fewer sulfites, it wouldn't explain most headaches. Sulfite sensitivity is real, but it mainly shows up as asthma-type symptoms (wheezing, chest tightness) in a small group of people, especially people who already have asthma. Headache is not the classic reaction.

There's also a simple kitchen test. Dried fruit like dried apricots and golden raisins usually contains far more sulfites than a glass of wine. If you can eat a handful of dried apricots with no headache but a glass of wine knocks you flat, sulfites are unlikely to be the culprit. We go deeper on this in our guide to [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

## The Real Reason #1: You Drink Differently in Europe

This is the biggest factor, and it's the least exciting one, which is probably why it gets ignored.

### Wine with food, almost every time

In Italy, France, Spain, and Portugal, wine is mostly a mealtime drink. You have a glass or two with a long lunch or dinner that might run two hours. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your bloodstream, which lowers your peak blood alcohol level. A lower peak generally means less of a hit the next morning.

Compare that to a common American pattern: a glass or two of wine before dinner, on an empty stomach, after a long workday. Same wine, very different effect.

### A slower pace

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, very roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies a lot between people. When you drink faster than that, alcohol and its toxic by-product, acetaldehyde, build up. Two glasses over two hours with a meal is a very different load from two glasses in 45 minutes.

### Smaller pours, and less in total

Restaurant and bar pours in much of Europe are often modest, commonly somewhere around 100 to 150 ml (about 3.5 to 5 ounces). At home, especially with large modern glasses, it's easy to pour 6 to 9 ounces and still call it "a glass." Two big home pours can quietly equal three or four standard drinks.

Many people also simply drink less on vacation than they think. You might have wine with lunch and dinner, but spread across a whole day of walking with water and food in between.

### Water on the table

In most European restaurants, a bottle of still or sparkling water arrives alongside the wine as a matter of course. Sipping water between glasses doesn't "flush out" alcohol, but it helps with dehydration, which is a real contributor to hangover headaches.

### More walking, more sleep, less stress

Vacations change everything about your day. You walk for hours, you sleep in, you're not answering work email at 11 p.m., and you're not waking at 6 a.m. to commute. Poor sleep and stress are both well-known headache triggers on their own, and alcohol already disrupts sleep. Taking work stress and a short night out of the equation can make the same amount of wine feel completely different the next day.

(Travel can cut the other way too. Long flights and jet lag can make headaches more likely in the first few days. That's another reason the "no headache" stories tend to come from the relaxed middle of a trip, not the first night.)

## The Real Reason #2: The Wine Itself Is Often Different

The wine you drink on a trip isn't a random sample of "European wine." It tends to be local, young, everyday wine, often lighter in style. Several real differences can matter.

### Alcohol percentage

Alcohol is the main driver of hangovers, so a percentage point or two adds up. Many popular American wines, especially big California reds, regularly land at 14% to 15% alcohol or higher. Plenty of European wines are lighter: think Beaujolais, many Loire reds, German Riesling, Vinho Verde, and lots of everyday table wine, which can sit around 11% to 13%.

This is not a clean Europe-vs-America split. Amarone, many Spanish reds, and wines from warm parts of Italy and southern France can be just as strong as anything from Napa. But if your vacation drinking skews toward house wine and lighter local styles, you may be taking in meaningfully less alcohol per glass.

There's also a labeling detail worth knowing. In the US, federal rules allow the stated alcohol on a wine label to be off by up to 1.5 percentage points for wines at 14% or below (and by 1 point above 14%), as long as it doesn't cross the 14% tax line. EU rules generally allow a much smaller margin, around half a percentage point. So a US bottle labeled 13.5% could legally be closer to 14.5% or more. It's worth treating the US number as an estimate.

### Sun, ripeness, and the quercetin idea

One of the more interesting recent theories about red wine headaches comes from researchers at the University of California, Davis. In a 2023 study published in *Scientific Reports*, they reported that **quercetin**, a natural plant compound found in grape skins, can be converted in the body into a form that blocks one of the enzymes that clears acetaldehyde. If acetaldehyde builds up, you can get flushing, headache, and nausea, similar to what some people experience after drinking.

What makes this relevant here: grapes make more quercetin when their clusters get lots of direct sunlight. The researchers suggested that sun-drenched grapes, which describes a lot of warm-climate red wine, could carry more quercetin than wine from cooler, cloudier regions. This was a lab study, and the team planned human trials to test it, so it's a hypothesis, not a settled answer. Still, it's a plausible reason why a lighter, cooler-climate red might treat you better than a ripe, sun-baked one, wherever either was made. Our [red wine headache guide](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) covers this research in more detail.

### Histamine and tyramine

Wine contains small amounts of histamine and related compounds called biogenic amines. Red wine usually has more than white. People who don't break down histamine efficiently can get headaches, flushing, a stuffy nose, or itchy skin from it. Histamine levels vary from wine to wine depending on the grapes, the bacteria involved in a second fermentation that softens the wine, and how carefully the winery works. There's no consistent evidence that European wine as a group has less histamine than American wine. If your symptoms look like this, read our page on [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol).

### Sugar and sweetness

Some popular mass-market American wines have a bit of residual sugar to make them taste smoother and fruitier, even when they aren't marketed as sweet. Sweetness can make wine easier to drink quickly and in larger amounts. Many everyday European table wines are fully dry. There is no good evidence that sugar itself causes headaches, but it can change how much and how fast you drink.

### Freshness and storage

Wine you drink in a winery region is often young, local, and hasn't been shipped across an ocean or sat in a hot warehouse. Heat-damaged wine tastes flat and off, but there's no good evidence that it causes more headaches. Consider this a minor factor at most.

## The Real Reason #3: Additives and Ingredient Rules

This is where the "American wine is full of chemicals" claim lives. The truth is more boring than the claim.

**Both the US and EU allow a long list of winemaking additives and processing aids.** These include things like added acid (tartaric acid), tannin powder, yeast nutrients, oak chips, fining agents that clear the wine (such as bentonite clay, egg white, or casein from milk), and concentrated grape juice used to adjust color or sweetness. Many of these are permitted in both places. The EU list is somewhat more restrictive in some areas, and specific European wine regions often add their own stricter rules on top, but "European wine is additive-free" is not true.

**Adding sugar before fermentation is allowed in parts of both.** This practice, called chaptalization, raises the final alcohol level when grapes aren't ripe enough. It's legal in cooler parts of Europe (including parts of France and Germany) and in some US states, while warm regions in both places, like California and much of southern Europe, generally don't allow it.

**The EU now requires more ingredient disclosure.** Wines made in the EU from December 2023 onward must list ingredients and nutrition information, though producers can put most of it behind a QR code on the label. Allergens such as sulfites, egg, and milk must still appear on the physical label. In the US, wine generally doesn't carry an ingredient list. That's a real transparency difference, but it's about what's *disclosed*, not proof of what's *in* the bottle. There's no evidence that the additives commonly used in US winemaking cause headaches at the amounts used.

**Pesticides and farming.** You'll see claims online that European wine has fewer pesticide residues. Rules on which farm chemicals are allowed do differ between the US and EU, but we're not aware of good evidence linking pesticide residues in wine to next-day headaches. If farming practices matter to you, look for certified organic or biodynamic wine from either side of the Atlantic.

## The Real Reason #4: Expectations and Memory

This sounds dismissive, but it isn't meant to be. Expectations shape how we feel. When you're on vacation, you're primed to feel good, and you're less likely to notice or remember a mild headache. At home, if you already believe wine gives you headaches, you're more likely to notice every twinge the next morning.

Memory also plays tricks. Two weeks of good mornings in Italy stand out. The one rough morning after a long dinner gets forgotten. Back home, the one bad headache after a work happy hour is what sticks.

None of this means your headaches are imaginary. It just means a trip abroad is a poor experiment, because everything changed at once: the wine, the pace, the food, the sleep, the stress, and your mood.

## Is It Better to Drink European Wine? What We Can Actually Say

Putting it together:

- There is no good evidence that European wine, as a category, causes fewer headaches than American wine.
- The differences that *do* exist (alcohol level, grape ripeness and sun exposure, style, labeling accuracy) vary more by region and producer than by continent.
- The way people drink in Southern Europe, with food, slowly, in modest pours, with water, is very likely the single biggest reason people feel better.

So if you love the European experience, the most useful thing to bring home isn't a case of Chianti. It's the habits.

## How to Drink Wine at Home Like You're in Europe

Here's a practical routine based on everything above.

1. **Drink wine with a real meal.** Not crackers, an actual dinner with protein, fat, and carbohydrates. This is the most effective single change for most people.
2. **Pour smaller.** Measure 5 ounces (150 ml) once so you know what it looks like in your glass. Many people are surprised by how much they've been pouring.
3. **Slow down to about a glass an hour or less.** Put the glass down between sips. Long dinners help.
4. **Keep water on the table.** Alternate a glass of water with each glass of wine.
5. **Check the alcohol percentage.** If you're sensitive, look for wines around 12% to 13% instead of 14.5% and up. Remember that US labels can be off by more than a point.
6. **Try lighter, cooler-climate styles.** Pinot Noir from cooler regions, Gamay (Beaujolais), many Loire Valley reds, dry Riesling, and crisp whites are good places to start. Our list of [wines that don't give you a headache](/never-hungover/wines-that-dont-give-you-a-headache) has more ideas.
7. **Protect your sleep.** Finish drinking a couple of hours before bed and don't cut your night short. A short night does more damage than people expect.
8. **Keep a simple log.** Write down the wine, its alcohol percentage, how much you had, whether you ate, and how you felt the next day. After a few weeks, patterns tend to jump out. You may find that one grape, one region, or one bottle size is the real problem.

If white wine is your trigger rather than red, our [white wine headache guide](/never-hungover/white-wine-headache) covers the different likely causes.

## When It's Probably Not the Wine, but You

Some people really do react to wine in a way that has nothing to do with where it came from:

- **Alcohol intolerance.** Some people, especially many people of East Asian descent, carry a gene variant that slows the clearing of acetaldehyde. Even a small drink can cause flushing, a fast heartbeat, nausea, and headache. Moving to Europe won't change that. See our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance).
- **Migraine.** Red wine is one of the best-known migraine triggers. If your headaches look like migraines, a doctor can help you figure out triggers and treatment.
- **Histamine intolerance.** Symptoms often include flushing, stuffy nose, hives, or itchy skin along with headache, and other high-histamine foods like aged cheese and cured meats may also bother you.
- **Sulfite sensitivity.** Rare, and usually shows up as wheezing rather than headache. People with asthma should take it seriously.
- **Medication interactions.** Some medicines interact with alcohol and can cause flushing, headache, or worse. If you take any regular medication, check with a pharmacist about alcohol.

If a single glass reliably gives you a headache, or your reactions are getting stronger, that's a reason to talk with your doctor instead of switching bottles.

## What About Hangover Supplements?

Some people use supplements to support a night of wine. One of the most studied is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal studies suggest it may help the body handle alcohol and its by-products, and some small human data are encouraging, but the research in people is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents wine headaches specifically, and it won't fix a migraine trigger, an intolerance, or an allergy. It also doesn't make it safe to drink more.

If you want to try it as one part of a sensible routine (with food, water, and moderate drinking), a simple, single-ingredient option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it and what the evidence does and doesn't show. Check with your doctor first if you take any regular medication.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does wine in Italy not give you a headache?**

Most likely because of how you drink there, not because Italian wine is fundamentally different. In Italy, wine usually comes with a long meal, in modest pours, with water on the table, and on vacation you're often walking more, sleeping more, and less stressed. Many everyday Italian wines are also lower in alcohol than big California reds. There's no study showing Italian wine causes fewer headaches.

**Does European wine have fewer sulfites than American wine?**

Not in a way that's likely to matter. Both use sulfites, and both require a "contains sulfites" warning. The EU's legal maximum is lower (about 150 mg/L for dry red and about 200 mg/L for dry white, versus 350 ppm in the US), but most quality dry wine in both places sits well below those limits. Sulfites also rarely cause headaches; sensitivity usually shows up as wheezing.

**Are there fewer chemicals and additives in European wine?**

Both the US and EU allow a range of additives and processing aids, such as added acid, tannin, yeast nutrients, and fining agents. The EU list is somewhat more restrictive in places, and many European wine regions add stricter rules, but European wine isn't additive-free. The EU now requires ingredient disclosure (often via a QR code), while most US wine doesn't list ingredients.

**Why do I get a headache from American red wine but not French wine?**

It may be the specific wines you're comparing. Ripe, warm-climate reds tend to be higher in alcohol, and research from UC Davis suggests sun-exposed grapes may carry more quercetin, a compound that may interfere with how your body clears acetaldehyde. Lighter French reds like Beaujolais or Loire reds are lower in alcohol and from cooler areas. A cool-climate American Pinot Noir might treat you just as well.

**Is organic or natural wine less likely to cause headaches?**

There is no good evidence that organic or natural wine causes fewer headaches. Organic wine usually has lower sulfite limits, but sulfites aren't a common headache cause. "Natural" wine has no legal definition in most places, and some natural wines can be higher in histamine. Alcohol content and how much you drink matter far more.

**How can I avoid wine headaches at home?**

Copy the European pattern: drink with a full meal, pour about 5 ounces, go slowly (about a glass an hour or less), alternate with water, choose lower-alcohol and cooler-climate wines, and protect your sleep. Keep a short log of what you drank and how you felt to find your personal triggers.

**When should I see a doctor about wine headaches?**

See a doctor if small amounts of wine reliably give you a headache, your headaches look like migraines, or you get flushing, hives, wheezing, or a racing heart with drinking. Get emergency care for a sudden, severe headache, or a headache with confusion, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, stiff neck, fever, or swelling of the face or throat.
